title: Indian Startup Funding Dips Below $100 Million as Deeptech Eyes Global Markets
excerpt: YourStory counted $96 million across 15 deals in a soft October week, while TechSparks panellists told deeptech founders that India alone is too small a market.
body:
• YourStory's tracker put Indian startup venture funding at $96 million across 15 deals in the week of October 17-23, down from $180 million the week before — the eighth sub-$100 million week of 2026.
  • Inc42's broader tally for October 19-23 counted $184 million across 17 deals, down 22% week on week; both trackers agree Even Healthcare's $50 million round was the week's anchor deal and that no $100 million-plus round closed.
  • Just 16 deals of $100 million or more have closed in India in all of 2026, according to YourStory.
  • At TechSparks 2026, deeptech founders said funding up to $5 million is now accessible, but $10-15 million growth cheques remain scarce — and that government demand alone cannot scale a deeptech company.

Indian startup funding fell sharply in the third week of October, and the week's other headline came from the stage at TechSparks 2026, where deeptech founders were told their market cannot be India alone.

YourStory's weekly roundup put venture capital funding at $96 million across 15 deals for October 17-23, down from $180 million the previous week. It was the eighth time in 2026 that a weekly total has fallen below $100 million. Inc42's tally for October 19-23, which counts a wider set of rounds, reached $184 million across 17 deals, down 22% from $236.2 million the week before. The two trackers use different windows and inclusion rules, but they agree on the shape of the week: activity slowed, and large cheques were absent.

One large deal, then a long tail

Even Healthcare raised $50 million from Khosla Ventures and Alpha Wave — a Series B in Inc42's table — accounting for more than half of YourStory's weekly total on its own. After that, YourStory's list drops quickly: The Pant Project raised about $11.4 million, rural healthcare platform CureBay about $10.4 million, Chapter Home about $6.6 million, traveltech startup TravClan $5 million and Hunar AI about $4.2 million.

Inc42's sector split shows where the money that did move went. AI startups raised $93.9 million across six deals — about half its weekly total, and the largest sector share for a second consecutive week — led by martech startup Different's $48 million round. Healthtech followed with $60.6 million across two deals, almost all of it Even and CureBay. Seed-stage startups raised $51.4 million, about 28% of Inc42's total.

The structural problem sits above those numbers. YourStory counted just 16 deals worth $100 million or more in India in all of 2026 so far, with the year drawing to a close — a thin pipeline of the large rounds that historically anchor weekly totals.

Deeptech told to go global

Against that funding backdrop, the TechSparks 2026 deeptech panel — founders from robotics, precision manufacturing and semiconductors, plus a policy executive — argued that India's deeptech companies must build for world markets from the start. Coverage in YourStory's TechSparks report described an ecosystem with improving government support, including a Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation Fund, but persistent gaps in talent, patient capital and manufacturing depth.

"India has the talent, scale and everything going for it. We just need to accelerate it at a feverish pace now."

— Shweta Rajpal Kohli, President & CEO, Startup Policy Forum, at TechSparks 2026

Kaushik Mudda, founder and CEO of precision manufacturing startup Ethereal Machines, said funding up to $5 million is no longer much of a challenge for deeptech startups, but the next rung — $10 million to $15 million — remains scarce. Gokul N A, founder of robotics startup CynLr, pointed to a shortage of quality mid-level engineering talent in a still service-oriented market. Agnit Semiconductors co-founder Hareesh Chandrasekar argued India needs sovereign semiconductor capability as chips become geopolitical leverage.

On the government's role, the panel drew a line: procurement can be a first buyer and a boost, as Kohli put it, but its process is complicated and it cannot be the only customer. Deep technology needs a global market, Gokul said — it cannot have India alone as its focus.

What to watch

For founders and diaspora investors watching Indian tech, the two stories connect. A funding market that produces few large rounds at home pushes exactly the advice the TechSparks panel gave: build companies whose revenue — and next fundraise — can come from global customers. YourStory closed its roundup by noting the ecosystem will be hoping for a revival in 2027. Whether that revival arrives will be visible first in the count of $100 million-plus deals, which has stalled at 16.
